passage:
Aadhya: How was Mummy today? She sounded so bright on the call
Avni: She sat by the phone from six, pretending to water the plants 😊
Aadhya: She said everything is fine
Avni: She always says that. She made your favourite dal yesterday and it's just the two of us
Aadhya: Didi is a terrible daughter, isn't she 🥺
Avni: No! But she lights up when your name comes on the screen. Then she hides it
Aadhya: I'll call at eight every evening, even for five minutes. And I'm booking the train for Diwali week
Avni: Don't tell her, let it be a surprise
Aadhya: Deal. Also tell her to stop watering the same plants 😅

qa.q: What did Mummy make yesterday that is Aadhya's favourite?
qa.a: Mummy made dal, which is Aadhya's favourite.

qa.q: What does Aadhya feel when Avni describes Mummy sitting by the phone?
qa.a: Aadhya feels guilty and tender, since she calls herself a terrible daughter and then decides to call more often.

qa.q: What choices does Aadhya make after reading Avni's messages?
qa.a: Aadhya decides to call at eight every evening, even for five minutes, and to book a train for Diwali week as a surprise.

qa.q: What is it like for Mummy when Aadhya's name comes on the screen?
qa.a: Mummy lights up, according to Avni, but then hides it and says everything is fine, perhaps so as not to burden Aadhya.

grounding: A parent at home lights up at a call and hides loneliness, and the young adult reads it and plans calls and a visit.

passage:
Arnab reached the village unannounced on Friday and stood at the gate for a minute. His father Anand sat on the veranda with a radio, but the radio was off and his eyes were on the road. When the phone rang inside, Anand was up and through the door before the second ring. Then, seeing Arnab, he smiled so widely that he forgot to say hello.
Over tea, Arnab said, "You never tell me you miss me."
"You are busy," said Anand, stirring his cup. "Why should an old man make it heavy?"
Arnab noticed the swept spare room and the jar of mango pickle labelled with his name. On Sunday, at the bus stop, he said, "Every Saturday at seven, I'll call. And I'll come in Poush month too." Anand nodded and looked at the bus, not at him.

qa.q: What did Arnab see inside the house that showed his father was expecting someone?
qa.a: He saw the swept spare room and a jar of mango pickle labelled with his name.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling when he noticed the swept spare room and the labelled pickle jar?
qa.a: He felt moved and a little guilty, realising his father misses him, which is why he promised regular calls and a visit.

qa.q: What could Arnab do to answer his father's quiet longing?
qa.a: Arnab promised a call every Saturday at seven and a visit in Poush month, giving his father regular things to look forward to.

qa.q: Why might Anand say 'Why should an old man make it heavy?'
qa.a: Anand may fear burdening Arnab with his loneliness, so he keeps quiet even though running to the ringing phone and the swept room show how much he waits for contact.

grounding: A parent at home hides loneliness and lights up at a call while the young adult reads the quiet longing and plans calls and visits.

passage:
Every Sunday at noon, Marek, twenty-five, video-called his mother, Valentina, in Kraków from his flat in Dublin. She always answered on the first ring, already smiling, hair brushed.
"I'm fine, everything's fine," she said, every time.
This Sunday, Marek noticed things. The table behind her was set for one. His father's chair was pushed against the wall. She laughed a little too quickly at his stories, and asked three times when his next holiday was.
"Mama, are you lonely?"
"Me? No, no. Busy, busy."
Marek looked at the single plate. He'd been so wrapped up in his new job that he'd left a gap of three weeks without calling.
"I'm booking a ticket for May," he said. "And let's talk Wednesdays too, not only Sundays."
His mother's smile wobbled. "Only if it's not a trouble."
"It isn't," Marek said.

qa.q: How many times did Valentina ask when his next holiday was?
qa.a: She asked three times when his next holiday was.

qa.q: What was Marek feeling when he looked at the single plate?
qa.a: Marek felt guilty and concerned, realising his mother was lonely and he had gone three weeks without calling.

qa.q: What steps did Marek take after reading the signs?
qa.a: He booked a ticket for May and added a Wednesday call, so his mother would feel less alone.

qa.q: What is it like for Valentina between calls?
qa.a: She seems lonely, setting the table for one, but she hides it so she won't burden Marek.

grounding: Outside India, a young adult abroad reads his mother's hidden loneliness during a call and responds by calling more and planning a visit.

passage:
Damini, twenty-four, home in Lucknow for Diwali, went with her father, Vikas, for his routine check-up. In the clinic waiting room, he told the man next to him, "My daughter works in Bengaluru. Software. Very big company." He said it twice.
When she went to fetch water, she heard him on the phone with a neighbour. "No, no, I'm fine alone. Damini calls sometimes."
Sometimes. Damini's chest tightened. She had been calling once every ten days, in a hurry.
Back in the waiting room, she noticed his shirt button was sewn with the wrong colour thread. Her mother had always done that.
"Papa, how are the evenings?" she asked.
"Fine, fine. TV. Walk." He looked at the floor.
On the train back, Damini set a reminder: call Papa every evening at eight, even for five minutes. And she booked a ticket home for his birthday.

qa.q: What did Vikas tell the man next to him?
qa.a: He said, "My daughter works in Bengaluru. Software. Very big company."

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when her chest tightened?
qa.a: Damini felt guilty and sad, realising that "sometimes" meant her father was lonely and missing her.

qa.q: What did Damini do after noticing the signs?
qa.a: She set a daily reminder to call Papa at eight and booked a ticket home for his birthday.

qa.q: How does Vikas seem to feel about being alone?
qa.a: Vikas seems proud of his daughter but lonely, hiding it with "fine, fine" and looking at the floor.

grounding: A young adult reads her father's quiet loneliness during a visit home and responds with regular calls and a planned visit.

passage:
Dear Amala,
Ganga Aunty from next door called me yesterday. She said you've been leaving the lamp on in my old room every night, and that you told her you "don't want to disturb" me with your worries.
Amala, I'm sorry. When we talk, you always say, "I'm fine, eat well, don't worry." I believed you because it was easy.
I remembered last month's call: you asked me twice what I'd had for dinner, and your voice went very quiet when I said I had to go.
So here's what I'm doing. I'll call you every evening after work, even for five minutes, and on Sundays we'll have tea together on video. And I've asked for leave for Losar. I'll be home for two weeks.
Please disturb me. I want to be disturbed.
Your Tenzin

qa.q: What has Amala been leaving on in the old room?
qa.a: She has been leaving the lamp on in Tenzin's old room every night.

qa.q: How does Tenzin feel after Ganga Aunty's call?
qa.a: Tenzin feels guilty and sorry, realising that Amala's "I'm fine" hid her loneliness.

qa.q: What plan does Tenzin make, and why does it help?
qa.a: Daily evening calls, Sunday video tea and two weeks home for Losar give Amala regular contact and something to look forward to.

qa.q: How might Amala feel when she reads "Please disturb me"?
qa.a: Amala would likely feel moved and relieved that her worries are welcome.

grounding: A young adult away from home learns of a parent's hidden loneliness and writes back promising regular calls and a visit.

passage: I'm Rekha, and this is something I only noticed this year. Every Sunday I call home from Hyderabad, and Appa's voice jumps ten feet when he hears it's me. "Rekha-ma! Eaten?" Then, very fast, he says everything is fine, the knees are fine, the neighbours are fine, go, go, you must be busy. For two years I believed him. Then in March my cousin sent a photo: Appa sitting alone on the verandah, two tumblers of coffee beside him, one untouched. That was Amma's habit, before she passed. I sat on the floor of my flat for a long time. Now I call on Wednesdays too, just to hear him complain about the milkman. And I've booked leave for Pongal. He said, "Why waste leave?" His voice was shaking.

qa.q: What did the cousin's photo show?
qa.a: It showed Appa sitting alone on the verandah with two tumblers of coffee beside him, one untouched.

qa.q: What does Rekha feel after seeing the photo?
qa.a: Rekha feels shaken and sad, sitting on the floor for a long time, seeing that Appa's cheerful "fine" was hiding loneliness.

qa.q: What did Rekha do once the quiet longing was clear?
qa.a: Rekha added a Wednesday call just to chat and booked leave for Pongal, giving regular contact and a visit.

qa.q: Why might Appa keep saying everything is fine?
qa.a: Appa probably does not want to burden Rekha and hides his loneliness out of love, though his shaking voice about the leave shows how much the visit means.

grounding: It illustrates a parent who lights up at a call but hides loneliness, and a young adult who reads it and calls more often and plans a visit.
